citation: Felix Rieseberg, 'Hunger beats tenure: Advice for junior engineers', felixrieseberg.com (personal blog, tagged 'management'), 27 October 2026. https://felixrieseberg.com/hunger-beats-tenure-advice-for-junior-engineers/ . Secondary: Gergely Orosz, 'The Pulse: Anthropic kills the coding interview', The Pragmatic Engineer newsletter, 30 October 2026 (paid issue). https://newsletter.pragmaticengineer.com/p/the-pulse-anthropic-kills-the-coding
evidence_tier: Practitioner post (first-person account by an Anthropic hiring manager on his personal blog; not an official Anthropic policy statement). The Pragmatic Engineer item is secondary press.
access_status: Rieseberg post: fully read (full HTML text retrieved 21 November 2026). Pragmatic Engineer: only the free portion read (title, subtitle, summary bullet and the lead-in sentence); the section quoting and analysing Rieseberg is paywalled ('This post is for paid subscribers').
sponsor_and_incentive: Self-published, no sponsor. Author is an engineering manager at Anthropic, which sells Claude and Claude Code; the post credits Claude with making coding tests pointless ('Claude is now better at both') and promotes Claude Code Desktop as 'a very popular product', so he has an employer interest in the AI-capability framing. Pragmatic Engineer is a paid newsletter; a dramatic headline drives subscriptions.
exact_quotes: Opening paragraph: 'This month, I laid the traditional coding interview to rest. As a hiring manager at Anthropic, I stopped asking candidates to do them. It had a good run: Being able to quickly define problems and find elegant solutions was a weak but useful predictor for how successful you'd be on my teams. Small coding challenges in real code did tell us something meaningful about candidates.'

Second paragraph: 'That's no longer true. There's no more point in giving you a little React challenge than there is in quizzing people about assembly; Claude is now better at both. Our most impactful builders are successful regardless of how good they are at these tests.'

Third paragraph: 'The coding interview was, despite its ubiquity, never popular.' ... 'Now that I've seen junior people work with AI for a bit, I have a more hopeful take: Impact is less bounded by how many years of accumulated knowledge in frameworks and libraries you've gathered.'
Fourth paragraph: 'I'm seeing engineers who are comparatively new fly past people who are probably better coders and have been around much longer. Hunger beats tenure.'
Fifth paragraph: 'This post is my best advice for junior engineers, though "junior" is the wrong word. It's really for engineers without social capital, status, or power.'
'All vision, no voice' section: 'Well, good news: Execution isn't expensive anymore.'
'What to do' (1): 'Pick business impact over backlog' (citing Patrick McKenzie, 2011: 'engineers are hired to create business value, not to program things.')
'What to do' (2): 'Pick a radical idea: Come up with a few ideas that would, if successful, dramatically improve the chances that your organization achieves those goals. Be ambitious!'

'What to do' (3): 'Build it over a weekend: I have seen small groups and solo engineers fly past the usual process of writing product requirements documents (PRDs), getting buy-in, and lobbying for time with designers or product managers by building a working prototype.'

'What to do' (4): 'Focus on one good idea' ... 'The point of creating a working prototype is to communicate an idea so well that leadership quickly understands both the opportunity and that you're the one who can run with it.'
'What to do' (5): 'Lean into your fresh perspective' ... 'you have a unique amount of empathy for users'.
'The future is bright' section: 'I don't think the coding interview is going to come back.'

Final paragraph: 'I'm probably not the only manager trying to figure out how to interview for people who build well with AI. I haven't quite gotten there yet — but I'm scanning resumes and portfolios for little prototypes that exhibit taste, empathy, and principled thinking. If you have figured out something better, I'd love to hear how.'
Author bio at foot of post: 'I'm an EM at Anthropic, where I've so far led engineering for Claude.ai, Cowork, and Claude Code Desktop.'

Pragmatic Engineer title: 'The Pulse: Anthropic kills the coding interview'. Subtitle: 'AI is rendering the Leetcode-style interview pointless and now Anthropic has deleted it from its interview loop.'

Pragmatic Engineer summary bullet: 'Anthropic kills its coding interview. A team at the leading frontier AI company gets zero signal from DSA interviews and so has removed it from the engineering recruitment process. The rest of the company, and other AI-native startups, could follow.'

Pragmatic Engineer section lead-in: 'A hiring manager at Anthropic who has led Claude Cowork and Claude Desktop, revealed that they have stopped asking coding questions to candidates for software engineering jobs. From Felix Rieseberg's blog post (emphasis mine):' [remainder paywalled]
date_and_recency: Post dated 27 October 2026; change made 'this month' (October 2026). Capability claim ('Claude is now better at both') refers to Claude as of October 2026, no model version named. Pragmatic Engineer summary dated 30 October 2026.
key_claims: He personally stopped giving traditional coding interviews in October 2026, as a hiring manager at Anthropic, for his own hiring.

Historically, the ability to 'quickly define problems and find elegant solutions' was 'a weak but useful predictor' of success on his teams, and small coding challenges 'in real code' told them something meaningful. Note the tense: he puts 'weak but useful' in the past and says 'That's no longer true.'
Claude now outperforms candidates on such tests (a 'little React challenge'), and the most impactful builders succeed regardless of how they score on them.
Impact is less bounded by years of accumulated framework and library knowledge; comparatively new engineers outpace better coders with longer tenure ('Hunger beats tenure').
Execution is no longer expensive, so engineers without status can win buy-in with a working prototype instead of PRDs and lobbying.
Main advice (five steps): pick business impact over backlog; pick a radical idea; build it over a weekend; focus on one good idea; lean into your fresh perspective.

He has not found a replacement interview format ('I haven't quite gotten there yet'); meanwhile he scans resumes and portfolios for little prototypes showing 'taste, empathy, and principled thinking', and invites better ideas.
He does not expect the coding interview to return.
headline_figures: No quantitative data. The only numbers are anecdotal: a Claude Code desktop prototype built by two relatively new engineers 'over one weekend', with 'The first public version shipped roughly eight days later'; Patrick McKenzie quote dated 2011; James March quote dated 1991.
'Weak but useful predictor' is a qualitative judgement, with no correlation coefficient or hiring-outcome data behind it.
sample_and_method: Personal experience and anecdote from one hiring manager's teams at Anthropic (plus earlier stints at Stripe, Notion, Slack). No systematic data, sample size, or outcome study. The subjects are software engineers.
what_is_measured: Old format: short coding challenges 'in real code' (e.g. a 'little React challenge'), measuring the ability to 'quickly define problems and find elegant solutions', which is convergent coding. Interim replacement (not an interview format): resume and portfolio screening for small prototypes that show 'taste, empathy, and principled thinking', in effect product judgement, user empathy and design reasoning, plus initiative ('hunger').
ai_policy_in_interview: Not stated as a policy. He removed the coding test instead of banning or permitting AI in it, reasoning that Claude outperforms candidates on it. No AI-use rule is described for the rest of his process.
scope_and_status: Applies to his own hiring ('I stopped asking candidates to do them'; predictor for 'my teams'). He leads engineering for Claude.ai, Cowork and Claude Code Desktop. Nothing in the post says Anthropic dropped coding interviews company-wide. Status: in place since October 2026, no replacement format yet.
validity_evidence: None. 'Weak but useful predictor' is his qualitative recollection, with no criterion-validity data. No evidence is offered for the portfolio-screening approach either.
relevance_to_angle: Supports 'stop testing convergent coding': a frontier-lab hiring manager dropped short coding tests because an AI model beats candidates on them. Partly supports the design-judgement angle ('taste, empathy, and principled thinking', 'principled thinking'). Complicates the essay's case: he has no replacement interview, he does not describe testing how candidates work with an agent, communication or team fit, and he admits the old test was a 'weak but useful' predictor, which concedes it had some value. Useful as a candid admission that the problem is unsolved.
limitations_stated: 'I haven't quite gotten there yet' (no replacement found); 'I'm probably not the only manager trying to figure out how to interview for people who build well with AI'; 'If you have figured out something better, I'd love to hear how.' He also concedes coding interviews once 'did tell us something meaningful about candidates.'
counter_evidence: His own words cut against the strongest version of the claim: the old interview was a predictor (weak, but useful), not useless. The secondary coverage inflates it. Pragmatic Engineer's headline 'Anthropic kills the coding interview' and subtitle 'Anthropic has deleted it from its interview loop' present a company-wide change, though its own summary says 'A team'. 'Zero signal from DSA interviews' and 'Leetcode-style' do not match Rieseberg, who described small real-code challenges (a React task, not data-structures-and-algorithms puzzles) as a weak but useful predictor in the past. Portfolio screening for side prototypes may favour candidates with spare time, a known equity concern with portfolio-based hiring (not raised in the post). The evidence is anecdotal and comes from someone at a company that sells the AI tool involved.
verification_status: All Rieseberg quotes, his role, scope, the 'weak but useful predictor' passage, 'taste, empathy, and principled thinking', the no-replacement admission and the five-step advice were checked against the primary post, opened in full on 21 November 2026. Pragmatic Engineer title, subtitle, summary bullet and lead-in were checked against the free portion of the page; its paywalled analysis was not read, so how it quotes or emphasises Rieseberg further is [uncertain].
